clue.text: Notice what disappointed examinee wants?

definitions.meaning: a notice or comment, as in a passing observation
a candidate unhappy with a grade wants the script marked again

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about what a let-down exam candidate hopes for.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition reads the answer as RE-MARK: marking the paper a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: A remark is a comment that notices something, and a re-mark is a second assessment of a script.

clue.text: Good shot right into mist — one croaks

parts.note: a bull is a hit on the bullseye, a good shot in darts or archery

indicators.note: into says the letter for right goes inside the word for mist

parts.note: fog is a thick mist

explanation.surface: A marksman's fine shot is fired into fog, and someone groans.
explanation.walkthrough: A bull is the bullseye on a target, so a 'good shot' in darts or archery.
explanation.definitionFit: A large frog is known for its deep croaking call, so it is something that croaks.

clue.text: Teacher gets into a flap about coffee-maker

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the whole assembled string is read backwards
gets into says the teacher's title goes inside the word for a flap

parts.note: a tab is a small flap, as on a label or envelope
Sir is how pupils address a male schoolteacher
taken as written

explanation.surface: A schoolteacher gets flustered over the coffee machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' turns round the whole string: the A, then the title for a teacher placed inside the flap. 'Flap' as panic is the misdirection; here it is a tab.
explanation.definitionFit: A barista is someone who prepares espresso drinks in a café, a person who makes coffee.

clue.text: Happen to secure expected standard: the best are beyond it

indicators.note: to secure means the word for happen holds the standard inside it

parts.note: come in the sense of come about, happen
par is the expected standard, as in golf

explanation.surface: Something reaches the expected level, but the finest go further.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the phrase 'beyond compare': the best things are beyond it. 'To secure' puts the standard inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Things described as beyond compare are peerless, so the very best lie past any comparison.

clue.text: No good to pick up list

indicators.note: No says the letter for good is removed from the word that follows

parts.note: to glean is to pick up or gather bit by bit

explanation.surface: A complaint that a useless roster is not worth collecting.
explanation.walkthrough: GLEAN without G gives the answer. 'List' looks like a roll of names but means tilt.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship that lists tilts to one side, which is what it means to lean.

clue.text: Some Protestants whip up tension against people

indicators.note: against means next to, so the two parts sit side by side

parts.note: men is a common crossword word for people

indicators.note: whip up means stir or churn, so the letters are mixed

explanation.surface: Agitators stir up trouble against the populace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whip up' makes NONITES from the clue word; 'against' just sets the two pieces next to each other.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mennonites are an Anabaptist Christian denomination, so they are one group of Protestants.

clue.text: Endless peace? Put a stop to boring farm work

indicators.note: Endless means the last letter of the word for peace is cut off

parts.note: hush is peace and quiet
to ban something is to put a stop to it
dry means dull or boring

explanation.surface: A farmer wants an end to the endless tedium of agricultural labour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' trims the word for peace to its first three letters. 'Farm work' is the old sense of husbandry, not anything marital.
explanation.definitionFit: Husbandry is the cultivation of crops and raising of animals, the work done on a farm.

clue.text: Apart from starter, fixed place to eat

indicators.note: Apart from starter means the first letter of the word for fixed is dropped

parts.note: stable means fixed, steady

explanation.surface: A diner talks of a set spot to eat, skipping the first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' suggests a first course, but it means the first letter of STABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A table is the piece of furniture at which people sit for a meal.

clue.text: Gangster abandons not really existing love of fine art

indicators.note: abandons says the gangster's name leaves the word that follows

parts.note: virtual means existing in effect but not in reality
Al Capone was the famous gangster, so Al stands for one

explanation.surface: A mobster gives up a fake passion for the arts.
explanation.walkthrough: Crosswords use AL for a gangster after Al Capone; 'abandons' takes those letters out.
explanation.definitionFit: Virtu is a taste for objets d'art and curios, a connoisseur's appreciation of fine things.

clue.text: Scientist naughtily Googles it

indicators.note: naughtily suggests misbehaving letters, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A researcher mischievously searches the web for a topic.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of GOOGLES IT are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A geologist studies the earth's rocks and structure, a kind of scientist.

clue.text: Extra chap that is finally squeezed in such a plane

parts.note: a wide is an extra in cricket, a run conceded for a ball bowled out of reach
bod is British slang for a person, a chap

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of the word squeezed

explanation.surface: An additional passenger is crammed into an aircraft of this type.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a wide is a ball out of the batsman's reach, giving the batting side an extra run.
explanation.definitionFit: A wide-bodied aircraft has a fuselage wide enough for two aisles, describing a kind of airliner.

clue.text: Old politician, foremost of wise heads in government

indicators.note: foremost of picks the first letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: An elder statesman leads the sage figures running the country.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letters of 'wise heads in government' spell the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Whigs were a British political party of the 17th to 19th centuries, so a member is a historical politician.

clue.text: In law, I see witch heartily burn

indicators.note: In says the letters for I and see go inside the word for law

parts.note: a rule is a law or regulation
taken as written
v is the abbreviation of vide, Latin for see

indicators.note: heartily picks the central letter of the word witch

explanation.surface: A ruling that a witch must be burnt at the stake.
explanation.walkthrough: I and V go inside RULE to make RIVULE, then T from the heart of 'witch'. 'Burn' is the Scottish word for a stream, not fire.
explanation.definitionFit: Burn is a Scottish and northern English word for a small stream, the same as a small brook.

clue.text: Ice-cream cut with tip of knife: it's rock-hard

indicators.note: cut means the end of the word for the iced dessert is lopped off

parts.note: a granita is an Italian iced dessert, loosely an ice-cream

indicators.note: tip of picks the end letter of the word knife

explanation.surface: Frozen dessert so solid you have to hack at it with a knife.
explanation.walkthrough: GRANITA loses its last letter, then E from the tip of 'knife'. The definition plays on granite as the rock of proverbial hardness.
explanation.definitionFit: Granite is a famously hard igneous stone, so it is the very type of rock-hard material.

clue.text: Once a week

parts.note: reads like 'weekly', but means a word that was formerly used for a period of seven days

explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' signals an archaic word: this is the old term for a week, contracted from seven nights.
explanation.definitionFit: Sennight, from seven nights, is an archaic English word for a week.

clue.text: Inhale smoke from source of fire

parts.note: a drag is a pull on a cigarette, inhaling smoke
one takes a drag on a cigarette, so on stands for from here

explanation.surface: A smoker takes a puff off a cigarette lit from a flame.
explanation.walkthrough: To drag on a cigarette is to inhale smoke from it.
explanation.definitionFit: Mythical dragons breathe flames, making them a fire-breathing beast in legend.

clue.text: Dissident perhaps is a little more bellicose

indicators.note: a little says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A protester is said to be somewhat more warlike.
explanation.definitionFit: A dissident opposes the established order, which is one kind of person who resists authority.

clue.text: One swimming in north Grasmere?

indicators.note: swimming means moving about freely, so the letters are mixed

explanation.surface: A creature seen paddling at the northern end of a Lake District lake.
explanation.walkthrough: N and GRASMERE are rearranged. Grasmere is a lake in England's Lake District, where this diving duck could well be found.
explanation.definitionFit: A merganser is a fish-eating diving duck found on lakes and rivers, so it swims.

clue.text: Plant providing strong drug experience

definitions.meaning: a marsh plant with tall stems, used for matting
the surge of euphoria felt after taking a drug

explanation.surface: A herb is said to give a powerful high.
explanation.definitionFit: A rush is a grass-like wetland plant, and also the sudden thrill from a narcotic.

clue.text: Not fly? Weird!

parts.note: un- is the prefix meaning not
fly is British slang for shrewd, knowing, which is canny

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims that it is strange an insect cannot fly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' looks like the insect or the verb but is the adjective meaning sharp-witted.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncanny means strange in an unsettling way, mysteriously weird.

clue.text: In test, rear of wall's replaced without protective cover

indicators.note: replaced says one part of the word for test is swapped out for another letter

parts.note: an examination is a test
ex is the Latin-derived prefix meaning without, as in ex dividend

indicators.note: rear of picks the end letter of the word wall

explanation.surface: An inspection finds the back of a wall has been rebuilt without any covering.
explanation.walkthrough: In EXAMINATION, 'replaced' swaps the EX ('without') for L, the rear of 'wall's'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lamination is a thin layer of plastic sealed over a document or surface to protect it.

clue.text: Heavily criticise opening of rotary drier

indicators.note: opening of picks the first letter of the word rotary

parts.note: an oast is a kiln for drying hops, familiar in Kent

explanation.surface: Harsh words about the start-up of a spinning clothes dryer.
explanation.walkthrough: An oast is a hop-drying kiln, a familiar building in the Kent countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: To roast someone is informal for criticising them severely.

clue.text: Backs away from big after-lunch nap, being most fat

indicators.note: Backs here means the back letter, the one at the end of each word, is taken off

parts.note: great means big

indicators.note: away from says that back letter goes away from the word for a nap, as from the word before

parts.note: a siesta is a nap taken after lunch, in Spain and elsewhere

explanation.surface: Someone abandons a long post-lunch sleep in favour of the fattiest food.
explanation.walkthrough: GREAT and SIESTA each lose their back letter, giving GREA + SIEST.
explanation.definitionFit: Greasiest means fattiest or most oily, the superlative of greasy.

clue.text: The last part, following task list? Not the last part

parts.note: f is the abbreviation for following, as in page references

indicators.note: Not the last part means the final letter of the word for a list of tasks is dropped

parts.note: an agenda is a list of items to be dealt with

explanation.surface: A riddle about the final stage of a to-do list.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The last part' appears twice: once as definition, once (with 'Not') as the signal to drop the final letter of the list. F stands for 'following' as in page references.
explanation.definitionFit: A fag end is British slang for a cigarette butt, and by extension the last, inferior remnant of anything.

clue.text: The reason the Romans had to fight?

definitions.text: The reason the Romans had to fight?

parts.words: The reason the Romans had to fight?
parts.note: reads as a history question but asks for the Latin phrase for a justification for war

explanation.walkthrough: The 'Romans' point to Latin: the phrase is the Latin term, still used in English, for a cause of war.
explanation.definitionFit: Casus belli is Latin for an occasion of war, an event used to justify going to war.

clue.text: Height: nothing dwarves can resolve in quarrel

indicators.note: can resolve means the letters may be worked out into a new order

parts.note: O is the figure zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Short folk settle arguments over nothing at a great height.
explanation.walkthrough: H, then O and DWARVES rearranged to AVEWORDS.
explanation.definitionFit: To have words with someone is the idiom for arguing or quarrelling with them.

clue.text: Spoiling start of Blackpool illuminations?

indicators.note: start of picks the first letter of the word Blackpool

parts.note: lighting is illumination

explanation.surface: Ruining the opening of a seaside town's famous light show.
explanation.walkthrough: Blackpool Illuminations are an annual autumn light display along the seafront of the English resort of Blackpool.
explanation.definitionFit: Blighting means ruining or spoiling, as a blight destroys crops.

clue.text: Share effort with wife

parts.note: a go is an attempt or effort
Dutch, short for duchess, is old Cockney slang for a wife, as in 'my old Dutch'

explanation.surface: A man splits the work with his spouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My old Dutch' is London Cockney slang for one's wife.
explanation.definitionFit: To go Dutch is to split the cost of a meal or outing, each sharing the bill.

clue.text: Where vertigo sufferers would be nervous?

definitions.meaning: at the brink of a cliff or drop, where fear of heights strikes

explanation.surface: People afraid of heights feel anxious near a drop.
explanation.definitionFit: On edge means tense and jumpy, and literally at the brink of a height.

clue.text: Finally booked fortnight or so, as suggested, over here?

indicators.note: Finally picks the last letter of the word booked
over means turned back to front, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: a fortnight is roughly half a month, here the first half of November's name

explanation.surface: Booking a two-week holiday on a friend's recommendation for this destination.
explanation.walkthrough: D, then NOVE (half of NOVEmber, a 'fortnight or so') reversed as EVON. The definition is the extended sense: a fortnight's booking for a classic English holiday county.
explanation.definitionFit: Devon is a county in south-west England, a popular destination for summer holidays.

clue.text: Part of village with a hole in it?

definitions.text: Part of village with a hole in it?

parts.words: Part of village with a hole in it?
parts.note: reads as a damaged bit of a village, but means the common grass of a village and the golf turf around a cup

explanation.walkthrough: The British village green is a common grassy area; a golf green is where the hole is.
explanation.definitionFit: A village has a communal grass area, and a golf putting surface has a hole in it.

clue.text: Pretty short supernatural being

indicators.note: short means the last letter of the word for a supernatural being is cut

parts.note: a fairy is a small magical being

explanation.surface: A tiny magical creature is described as attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: FAIRY is cut short by its last letter. 'Short' looks like a description of the fairy's height.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair is an old-fashioned word for good-looking, attractive.
